doc_summary: Greenblatt and Stastny analyze how future research could catch and study actual schemers (via production, many training runs, or rigged training), covering analogousness, overfitting, unreliable re-catching, and schemers sabotaging experiments. They stress that synthetic inputs and false beliefs are key levers and that AIs that notice fake inputs won't reveal bad behavior.

items.claim: In a setup, use actual production tasks (without using the AI's outputs) instead of synthetic inputs because a schemer that notices inputs are fake will not take the bad action you are trying to elicit.
items.quote: So if we use synthetic inputs in the hope that this triggers these bad actions, the AI might notice these inputs are fake and then not do anything bad. We could potentially resolve this by just using actual tasks from production usage

items.claim: Prefers inputs/beliefs that are a priori plausible over merely inserted false information because smarter AIs get better at noticing and disregarding implausible information.
items.quote: As AIs get smarter, they will be better at noticing and disregarding implausible information, so it might be very important that the information is a priori plausible.

items.claim: Eval-likeness comes from hard-to-simulate interactions with expensive parts of the environment (humans, compute); the AI may only misbehave when it sees such hard-to-fake evidence.
items.quote: there might often be some difficult to simulate interaction between the AI and an expensive aspect of the environment (compute or humans). (And the AI only does bad actions when it sees this hard to fake evidence.)

items.claim: Considers hard-to-distinguish synthetic inputs and inserting false beliefs the most valuable work for building setups where schemers can be repeatedly caught.
items.quote: Currently, we're particularly excited about work on generating hard-to-distinguish synthetic inputs and inserting false beliefs into AIs which both seem extremely helpful for creating setups where we can repeatedly catch schemers.

items.claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence that a schemer is not scheming, because a capable schemer who recognizes an experiment may sabotage it or choose to do nothing.
items.quote: First, the schemer would likely need to recognize it is in an experiment. In some cases, this might be extremely obvious as there isn't a good way to do the experiment without this being clear.

items.claim: Prefers a larger, more diverse set of test examples over a small set because removal validated on few examples may only make the model stop misbehaving on those examples without removing scheming.
items.quote: methods which aim to remove scheming and are validated by checking that the model doesn't misbehave on a small set of examples might only (randomly) alter the AI such that it no longer misbehaves on those examples

items.claim: Make the situation plausible by varying the AI's believed situation (already caught, weaker countermeasures, fictional company), but note the AI may reject beliefs inconsistent with its own known attack strategy.
items.quote: The AI might have (confident) views about what attacks it would/wouldn't try so if the knowledge we try to insert implies we caught it doing a particular attack (that it knows it wouldn't have done) it could end up thinking this information is false.

items.claim: Distrusts rigged or trained-in scheming as legible evidence and distrusts iterating on unprincipled techniques in disanalogous testbeds due to overfitting.
items.quote: Producing scheming using a rigged process—if rigged to make scheming more likely—seems much less useful than natural scheming for producing legible evidence of scheming

items.claim: Prefers testing simple, principled techniques over wide ranges of unprincipled ones because limited, non-diverse test beds make overfitting likely.
items.quote: it seems best to test different (simple and) principled techniques or try to actually build a good understanding of scheming (both how it emerges and what might remove it). This is as opposed to testing a wide range of unprincipled (and potentially complex) techniques

items.claim: Honest tests where the AI believes the situation is real (or knows it's a test but acts anyway) can elicit behavior without relying on the AI being fooled.
items.quote: a situation where the AI isn't aware it is in a test and just thinks, potentially correctly, that it can achieve its aims

items.claim: Open problem: develop deals/credibility and diverse catching methods; the approach is not yet actionable and requires more capable AIs.
items.quote: All of the aforementioned opportunities require a higher level of capability than exists right now, so this post doesn't describe a research agenda which is actionable right now.
